title: Polylogarithmic approximation for Directed Steiner Tree
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
formal:
Do there exist positive integers \(a,C,K,q\) and one uniform randomized classical algorithm \(A\) such that, for every feasible Directed Steiner Tree instance \(I\) of encoding length \(N\) with \(k\ge1\) terminals, every execution halts within \(K(N+1)^q\) bit steps and outputs a feasible arc subset \(F\), and
\[\Pr\!\left[c(F)\le a\bigl(\log_2(k+2)\bigr)^C\operatorname{OPT}(I)\right]\ge\frac23?\]
The probability is over the algorithm’s internal randomness, separately for each input. The graph is arbitrary and directed, with exactly represented nonnegative rational arc costs. All four constants and the program must be independent of the instance.
definitions:
Instance. The vertex set is \(V=[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), where \(n\ge2\). A finite list of \(m\) indexed arcs specifies their tails and heads in \(V\); different indices denote different arcs even when their endpoints coincide. Loops and parallel arcs are allowed. The root is \(r\in V\), and the terminal set is \(T\subseteq V\setminus\{r\}\), with \(k=|T|\ge1\). Every arc \(e\) has cost \(c_e=u_e/v_e\), where \(u_e\) is a nonnegative integer and \(v_e\) a positive integer, both supplied in binary. Zero costs and arbitrarily long cost descriptions are allowed. There is no planarity, acyclicity, degree, treewidth, depth or metric promise.

Reachability and feasibility. A directed path follows arc orientations from its first vertex to its last; it may be taken without repeated vertices. The input is promised feasible: every terminal is reachable from \(r\). A feasible output is a subset \(F\subseteq E\) of arc indices such that the subgraph \((V,F)\) has a directed \(r\)-to-\(t\) path for every \(t\in T\). Nonterminal vertices may be used freely as intermediate vertices. Arc cost is paid once, regardless of how many terminal paths use it:
\[c(F)=\sum_{e\in F}c_e,\qquad\operatorname{OPT}(I)=\min\{c(F):F\subseteq E\text{ is feasible}\}.\]
The minimum exists because there are finitely many subsets and at least one is feasible. It may equal zero. The name “tree” does not impose an additional output-syntax condition: a feasible directed subgraph qualifies. Nonnegative costs also permit deletion of redundant arcs to obtain a rooted outward branching without increasing cost. Terminals are not required to be leaves.

Encoding and size. The graph, root, terminal list and every arc cost are explicit. One fixed encoding lists \(n,m,r,k\), all vertex labels \(1,\ldots,n\), the \(k\) distinct terminal labels in increasing order, and, for each indexed arc in order, its tail, head, numerator and denominator. Encode each nonnegative integer by its binary expansion preceded by its length in unary and a zero delimiter; the expansion of zero is the single bit zero. Let \(N\) be the total bit length. In particular \(N\ge n\), and every bit of every cost contributes to \(N\). Output identifies the selected arc indices, or equivalently their \(m\)-bit indicator vector.

Computation and randomness. Use an ordinary uniform multitape Turing machine with a finite program, read-only input, initially blank work tapes and a write-only output tape. A step reads and updates a constant number of tape symbols and moves each head by at most one cell; a random step additionally supplies one independent fair bit. Reading the input, writing the entire solution, exact rational arithmetic and all preprocessing count in the bit time. No nonuniform advice, free optimization oracle, supplied fractional solution or unit-cost exact-real operation is available. The required bound holds for every random bit sequence, not just on average.

Guarantee. On each feasible input, every execution must return a feasible subset; on an event of probability at least \(2/3\), its cost must also satisfy the displayed ratio. On other executions the cost may be larger but feasibility is still required. When \(\operatorname{OPT}=0\), the successful output must have cost zero; an additive positive error is not allowed. The \(k+2\) convention makes the factor defined and positive also at one terminal. Choosing positive integer constants rather than arbitrary real constants at least one does not change existence, since the logarithm is greater than one and rounding constants upward only relaxes the bound. No behavior is prescribed on malformed encodings; infeasible well-formed instances may be detected and reported in polynomial time before applying the feasible-instance algorithm.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence claim or its negation. For a positive answer, specify an algorithm and fixed constants, and prove its bit running time on every execution, feasibility of every output, and the per-instance probability and cost bound throughout the full class. The proof must account for binary rational costs and zero optimum. A procedure with a variable time exponent depending on \(k\), or with uncharged access to a special fractional solution, does not meet the statement.

A negative answer must rule out every fixed power \(C\) of \(\log_2(k+2)\), every factor \(a\), every polynomial time bound and every permitted randomized program. For example, for every uniformly polynomial-time program that always returns feasible outputs and for every \(a,C\), it suffices to prove the existence of a feasible instance on which the probability of the requested ratio is less than \(2/3\). A lower bound for deterministic programs alone is insufficient. A conditional hardness theorem must identify its unproved assumptions and does not by itself give an unconditional negative answer.

A polylogarithmic ratio in quasipolynomial time, an \(O(k^{\varepsilon})\) ratio for each separately fixed \(\varepsilon>0\), a theorem for planar graphs, or an integrality gap for one chosen relaxation is partial progress. Hardness below a particular logarithmic power leaves larger fixed powers possible. Expected-time or expected-cost analyses must be converted into the stated execution-time and success guarantees in the checked proof; they cannot simply replace those requirements.
why: A defining gap in directed network-design approximation: determine whether a shared directed connection network can be approximated within a polylogarithmic factor using only polynomial time.

importance.reason: A central approximation problem encompassing covering and rooted network design, with a persistent gap between polynomial and quasipolynomial algorithms.

progress.text: Classical directed Steiner approximation algorithms give \(O(k^{\varepsilon})\) for every fixed \(\varepsilon >0\) in polynomial time.
Grandoni–Laekhanukit–Li obtain \(O(\log ^{2} k/\log  \log  k)\) in quasipolynomial time, with conditional matching-scale hardness.
Friggstad–Mousavi obtain a polynomial-time \(O(\log  k)\)-approximation for planar digraphs.
Chekuri and coauthors extend planar rooted-network techniques and prove an \(O(\log ^{2} k)\) planar LP gap.
Version 2 of Laekhanukit’s initial general claim is withdrawn.
Version 3 narrows the claim to an expected-polynomial-time result with access to a relatively integral fractional solution; the record retains its withdrawal comment.

Chekuri–Jain’s planar length-constrained bicriteria results are posted in July and published at APPROX/RANDOM in September. The published introduction still retains the general polynomial-time polylogarithmic DST question.

status_note: Checked through 16 September 2026. The 9 September APPROX/RANDOM publication explicitly retains the general polynomial-time polylogarithmic DST approximation problem as open. The inherited 2024 general claim was withdrawn; its October 2025 replacement assumes a special supplied fractional solution and states expected polynomial time, while the record still displays the withdrawal comment. Planar bicriteria and quasipolynomial algorithms do not meet the full card. No matching general resolution was found in the bounded primary-source search; external proofs were not independently certified.

context_blocks.text: The problem asks how cheaply a root can reach many destinations through one shared directed network. Buying a common initial segment can save cost across many root-to-terminal paths, but the directions restrict which branching structures are usable. With one terminal the problem is shortest path. With many terminals, selecting where the paths should share infrastructure becomes the central optimization challenge.

A simple reduction explains why ordinary reachability is insufficient. For a set-cover instance, create a vertex for each set and each element, an arc of cost one from the root to every set vertex, and zero-cost arcs from each set to its elements. Make all element vertices terminals. A feasible network must buy a collection of set arcs covering all elements, and its cost equals the number of chosen sets. The directed graph can thus encode a nontrivial covering problem even with only two layers after the root.

The familiar polynomial-time approximation frontier is \(O(k^{\varepsilon})\) for every fixed \(\varepsilon >0\), from the classical directed Steiner algorithms. The running-time exponent depends on the chosen accuracy parameter. Setting \(\varepsilon\) to a quantity that shrinks with k is not a free improvement: it changes that dependence and can produce quasipolynomial time. A power of k, however small and fixed, eventually exceeds every fixed power of log k.

Grandoni, Laekhanukit and Li prove a randomized \(O(\log^2 k/\log\log k)\) approximation with running time \(n^{O(\log^5 k)}\), in the asymptotic range where this expression is used. This is quasipolynomial: its exponent grows with the input parameter. The target here permits a larger fixed power of the logarithm, but requires one polynomial time exponent for every instance. The old classical paper’s original quasipolynomial \(O(\log^2 k)\) claim was corrected to \(O(\log^3 k)\) because of a height-reduction lemma; the 2019 paper explicitly records that correction.

The same work gives near-matching quasipolynomial-time hardness under additional complexity assumptions, including the Projection Games Conjecture. This does not show that every polynomial-time polylogarithmic approximation is impossible: a larger fixed logarithmic power is allowed in this card. The issue is a gap between what can currently be computed in polynomial time and what is known with more time, rather than the already settled hardness of exact optimization.

A natural flow relaxation buys a fractional capacity \(x_{e}\) for each arc and, separately for each terminal, sends a unit flow from the root using at most \(x_{e}\) on that arc. Different terminals may reuse the same purchased capacity because a network edge is bought once. In general graphs this relaxation has polynomial-size integrality gaps, including \(\Omega (\sqrt{k})\) examples. Those examples explain why a straightforward LP-rounding strategy cannot guarantee a polylogarithmic factor against that relaxation on every instance. They do not rule out stronger relaxations or a different algorithm.

The December 2024 general approximation claim was withdrawn in version 2. Version 3, submitted in October 2025, calls itself a rectification and assumes access to a relatively integral solution of a strengthened relaxation: for each terminal and arc, its flow is either zero or the whole purchased capacity. Theorem 1 states an expected-polynomial-time rounding result under this extra hypothesis. This is neither an algorithm that supplies the needed solution on every ordinary input nor a proof for arbitrary standard flow-LP optima. The live record still carries the reachability-proof withdrawal comment. The restricted result is recorded as a reported claim, not an independently verified general approximation.

Planarity changes the picture substantially. Friggstad and Mousavi give a polynomial-time \(O(\log  k)\)-approximation for planar directed graphs, using shortest-path separators. Later work extends the structural approach to other rooted planar network-design problems and bounds a natural planar LP gap by \(O(\log ^{2} k)\). These theorems show that directedness alone does not preclude the requested factor, but their separator arguments do not apply to arbitrary directed graphs.

Chekuri and Jain’s length-constrained work appeared on arXiv in July and was published on 9 September 2026. The published introduction still explicitly identifies the general polynomial-time polylogarithmic DST question as open. For planar graphs, Theorem 2 gives logarithmic cost approximation with logarithmic length slack, while Theorem 3 gives a log-squared bound against a fractional relaxation with the same length slack. Removing the path-length constraint does not remove their planarity assumption. The related directed-forest theorem has multiple source–sink demands, a different target from one-root DST.

sentences: Directed Steiner Tree seeks a minimum-cost directed subgraph connecting one root to every designated terminal.
The target is one uniform randomized algorithm with a fixed polynomial bit running time and a fixed polylogarithmic approximation factor in the number of terminals.
Every output must be feasible, and each input must achieve the cost guarantee with probability at least two thirds, including instances with zero optimum.
A complete Lean proof must establish those guarantees or rule out all permitted randomized algorithms and all fixed logarithmic powers.
The September 2026 published literature still leaves this general problem open; planar algorithms, quasipolynomial results and the corrected fractional-solution claim have additional restrictions.

source_formulation.text: The inherited 2024 Laekhanukit entry once claimed a general polynomial-time polylogarithmic approximation. That claim was withdrawn, and the October 2025 replacement expressly assumes access to a relatively integral solution of a strengthened relaxation. This card retains the underlying general approximation question, not the restricted replacement theorem. The existing terminal-count factor, randomized success convention, always-feasible output, nonnegative rational costs, category and importance 96 are preserved; the review specifies the bit model and complete quantifier order.
